Creates sub-communicators of 4 consecutive ranks each
Duplicates MPI_COMM_WORLD four times
Removes every fourth rank from MPI_COMM_WORLD
questions.explanation: Processes with the same color end up in the same new communicator, ordered by the key. Here ranks 0-3 form one group, 4-7 the next, and so on.

questions.text: An MPI program calls MPI_Comm_rank and MPI_Comm_size on MPI_COMM_WORLD and is launched with mpirun -np 4. What values do they report?
options: Ranks 1 to 4, and size 4
Ranks 0 to 3, and size 4
Ranks 0 to 4, and size 5
Every process reports rank 0, and size 4
questions.explanation: MPI_Comm_size gives the number of processes in the communicator. Each process gets a distinct rank starting from 0.

questions.text: What is the purpose of MPI_Finalize()?
options: To send any final messages to the root process
To combine the final results from all processes
To clean up the MPI environment after all MPI work is complete
To act as a barrier that guarantees all output is printed
questions.explanation: Every process calls it once at the end, after completing its communication. Most MPI calls are not allowed afterwards.

questions.text: When a blocking MPI_Send returns, what is guaranteed?
options: The receiver has received and processed the message
The send buffer can be safely reused
The matching receive has been posted
The message has been written to disk
questions.explanation: Standard-mode MPI_Send may return after copying the data into a system buffer or only after the receiver starts receiving. Either way, only buffer reuse is guaranteed.

questions.text: A process calls MPI_Isend on a buffer. When may it safely modify that buffer?
options: Immediately after MPI_Isend returns
Once MPI_Wait or MPI_Test reports completion
After the receiving process calls MPI_Finalize
Never, because the buffer belongs to MPI from then on
questions.explanation: A nonblocking send only starts the operation. Until the request completes, MPI may still be reading the buffer, so changing it could corrupt the message.

questions.text: How does MPI_Test differ from MPI_Wait?
options: MPI_Test sends a test message; MPI_Wait sends real data
MPI_Test checks without blocking; MPI_Wait blocks until done
MPI_Test works only for sends; MPI_Wait only for receives
MPI_Test cancels the operation if it is not finished
questions.explanation: MPI_Test sets a flag and returns immediately, so a process can do other work and check again later. MPI_Wait is the blocking choice.

questions.text: When does a synchronous-mode send, MPI_Ssend, complete?
options: As soon as the data is copied into a system buffer
Only after the matching receive has started
Only after the receiver has finished processing the data
Immediately, like a nonblocking send
questions.explanation: MPI_Ssend never completes by buffering alone. Testing code with it reveals programs that only work because the implementation happens to buffer messages.

questions.text: Two ranks each call MPI_Send to the other with a large message, then MPI_Recv. What can happen, and what is a standard fix?
options: Nothing can go wrong, because MPI always buffers sends
Both may wait forever; use MPI_Sendrecv instead
The messages are swapped automatically, so the code is safe
MPI reports an error, so the ranks must use MPI_Bcast instead
questions.explanation: Large messages often are not buffered, so each MPI_Send waits for the other's receive, creating a cycle. MPI_Sendrecv lets MPI handle both directions without deadlock; ordering the calls oppositely on the two ranks also works.

questions.text: What does MPI_Barrier(comm) guarantee?
options: All pending messages in the communicator are delivered
No process leaves it until every process has entered it
Only one process at a time can send messages afterwards
All processes print their output in rank order
questions.explanation: A barrier is an explicit synchronization point. It says nothing about message delivery and should not be used to patch an unclear communication design.

questions.text: Can a collective such as MPI_Bcast be relied on as a substitute for MPI_Barrier?
options: Yes, every collective synchronizes all processes like a barrier
No, it may return before other processes have entered it
Yes, as long as the root process is rank 0
No, because collectives can be called by only some processes
questions.explanation: Every process in the communicator must make the matching call, but only MPI_Barrier guarantees that all have arrived. A broadcast root, for example, may return as soon as its buffer can be reused.

questions.text: What is collective communication in MPI?
options: A message exchanged between exactly two processes
An operation every process in the communicator must call
Communication that uses shared memory instead of messages
Messages exchanged between two separate MPI jobs
questions.explanation: Collectives express group patterns directly, which makes intent clear and lets the implementation use efficient tree or ring algorithms.

questions.text: What does MPI_Bcast() do?
options: Broadcasts a message to every computer on the network
Copies the root's data to every process in the communicator
Sends a different piece of data to each process
Collects one value from every process at the root
questions.explanation: After the call, every process has a copy of the root's buffer. Scattering different pieces is MPI_Scatter.

questions.text: Four ranks hold the values 4, 7, 2 and 9 and call MPI_Reduce with MPI_SUM and root 0. What is the result?
options: Rank 0 receives 22
Every rank receives 22
Rank 0 receives 4, its own value
Each rank receives the sum of the values before it
questions.explanation: MPI_Reduce combines the values with the given operation and stores the result only at the root. MPI_Allreduce would give 22 to every rank.

questions.text: How does MPI_Allreduce differ from MPI_Reduce?
options: It works on all MPI data types, not only on integers
Every process receives the reduced result, not just the root
It is nonblocking, while MPI_Reduce is blocking
It reduces the data from every communicator in the job at once
questions.explanation: All-reduce is common when every process needs the global value, such as a convergence norm in a simulation or summed gradients in distributed training.

questions.text: What is the difference between MPI_Scatter and MPI_Gather?
options: Scatter is meant for small messages, while Gather is for large ones
Scatter splits root data among processes; Gather collects pieces at the root
Scatter is synchronous; Gather is asynchronous and returns early
Scatter sends the same data everywhere; Gather sums the data
questions.explanation: They are inverse patterns. A typical program scatters chunks of an array, lets each process work on its chunk, then gathers the results.

questions.text: What does MPI_Alltoall do?
options: Broadcasts one buffer from every process to the root
Every process sends a distinct block of data to every other process
Reduces data from all processes and broadcasts the result
Synchronizes all processes without exchanging data
questions.explanation: All-to-all is a complete exchange, used for example in distributed matrix transposes and FFTs. Its cost grows quickly with process count.

questions.text: Ranks 0-3 contribute the values 1, 2, 3 and 4 to MPI_Scan with MPI_SUM. What does rank 2 receive?
questions.explanation: MPI_Scan is an inclusive prefix reduction: rank i receives the combination of values from ranks 0 to i. Rank 2 gets 1 + 2 + 3 = 6.

questions.text: What are message tags used for in MPI?
options: Labelling messages so debuggers can display them
Distinguishing kinds of messages between the same processes
Selecting how the message's header is compressed in transit
Choosing the key used to encrypt the message
questions.explanation: A receive matches on communicator, source and tag. Distinct tags let a process receive, for example, data messages and control messages separately.

questions.text: Rank 0 receives from ranks 1 and 2 with MPI_ANY_SOURCE. Why might the output differ between runs?
options: MPI_ANY_SOURCE drops one of the messages at random
Messages from different senders can arrive in either order
MPI reorders the messages from each sender
MPI_ANY_SOURCE only works with blocking sends
questions.explanation: Arrival order across senders depends on timing. Naming the expected source rank, and a specific tag, removes the ambiguity when the program needs a fixed order.

questions.text: Rank 1 sends two messages to rank 0 with the same tag and communicator. In what order can rank 0 receive them?
options: In the order they were sent
In any order, depending on network timing
Only the second one, which overwrites the first
In order of message size, smallest first
questions.explanation: MPI guarantees that matching messages between the same sender and receiver do not overtake each other. It gives no ordering guarantee across different senders.

questions.text: Why might a process call MPI_Probe before MPI_Recv?
options: To check whether the network link is working
To learn an incoming message's size before allocating a buffer
To test whether the sending process is still alive
To measure the round-trip network latency to the sender
questions.explanation: MPI_Probe returns a status describing a matching message without receiving it. MPI_Get_count on that status gives its size, so the buffer can be allocated exactly.

questions.text: A receive specifies a count of 100 elements, but the matching message has 60. What happens?
options: MPI reports an error because the counts differ
It succeeds, and MPI_Get_count reports 60
The remaining 40 elements are filled with zeros
The receive waits for 40 more elements
questions.explanation: The receive count is a capacity, so it can exceed the message size. Receiving a message larger than the buffer is the error case.

questions.text: What is a Cartesian topology in MPI?
options: The physical layout of cables in a cluster
A virtual grid of processes, in 1D, 2D or 3D
A row-major memory layout for storing matrices
A visualisation produced by MPI debugging tools
questions.explanation: MPI_Cart_create builds the grid and MPI_Cart_shift finds neighbor ranks, which suits grid-based simulations; dimensions can be periodic. Virtual topologies do not change where processes physically run.

questions.text: Why use an MPI derived datatype such as MPI_Type_vector to send a matrix column?
options: It compresses the column's data before sending it
It describes the strided layout, so no manual packing is needed
It transposes the column into a row on the receiving side
It is the only way MPI can send floating-point data
questions.explanation: In a row-major matrix, a column's elements are not contiguous. A vector type with the right stride lets MPI read them directly.

questions.text: What are ghost (halo) cells in a domain-decomposed simulation?
options: Cells that store data deleted during the simulation
Local copies of neighbors' boundary values
Unused cells added to pad arrays to a power of two
Cells that record errors detected during communication
questions.explanation: A stencil near the edge of a subdomain needs neighbor values. Each step, processes exchange their boundary data to refresh these halo copies.

questions.text: What is latency hiding in distributed computing?
options: Hiding network delays from users with a progress bar
Overlapping communication with independent computation
Compressing messages so they arrive sooner
Caching every remote value locally in advance
questions.explanation: A process can post nonblocking sends and receives, compute work that does not depend on them, and only then wait. Actual overlap depends on the MPI implementation making progress.

questions.text: What does the CAP theorem say about distributed data stores?
options: They can guarantee consistency, availability and partition tolerance at all times
During a network partition, a system must choose between consistency and availability
Caching, availability and performance cannot be optimised together
Replication always reduces both consistency and availability
questions.explanation: Partitions cannot be ruled out in real networks. While one lasts, a node must either refuse requests (keeping consistency) or answer with possibly stale data (keeping availability).

questions.text: What is eventual consistency?
options: Every read always returns the latest write
If updates stop, all replicas eventually converge to the same value
Data becomes consistent only after the whole system restarts
Writes are applied to all replicas in one fixed global order
questions.explanation: Replicas may temporarily disagree, so a read can return stale data. Many highly available systems accept this in exchange for lower latency and partition tolerance.

questions.text: What is a primary trade-off of replicating data across nodes?
options: It always reduces the latency of every single write
It improves availability and reads but makes consistency costlier
It removes any need to handle node or link failures
It only benefits write-heavy workloads
questions.explanation: More copies mean more places to read from and survive failures, but every write must be propagated and conflicts resolved.

questions.text: What is sharding?
options: Copying the full dataset to every node
Partitioning data so each node holds only a subset
Compressing data before it is stored on disk
Caching data only at the network edge
questions.explanation: Each shard owns a range or hash of keys, so storage and writes scale out. Queries that span many shards become more expensive, so the shard key is chosen to keep common queries local.

questions.text: What makes failure handling fundamentally different in a distributed system than on a single machine?
options: Distributed systems never experience hardware failures
Partial failure: one node or link can fail while the rest keeps running
A failure on any node always stops the whole system immediately
Failures can only occur in the network, never in nodes
questions.explanation: A slow or silent node is hard to distinguish from a crashed one. Systems therefore use timeouts, retries, replication and checkpointing to keep working.

questions.text: How does a typical cluster differ from a general distributed system?
options: Its nodes are usually colocated and centrally managed
Its machines all share one physical memory
It cannot run tightly coupled MPI programs
It must consist of identical hardware nodes
questions.explanation: A cluster is a kind of distributed system. Its low-latency interconnect and shared scheduling make tightly coupled jobs such as MPI simulations practical, and heterogeneous CPU/GPU clusters are common.

questions.text: Flynn's taxonomy classifies computer architectures by the number of concurrent _ streams and ___ streams.
options: input; output
instruction; data
program; memory
cache; I/O
questions.explanation: Combining single or multiple instruction streams with single or multiple data streams gives the four classes SISD, SIMD, MISD and MIMD.

questions.text: In Flynn's taxonomy, which class describes a modern multicore PC across its cores?
options: SISD
SIMD
MISD
MIMD
questions.explanation: Each core runs its own instruction stream on its own data. Inside each core, vector instructions also provide SIMD, so real systems often combine classes.

questions.text: Which is a typical example of SIMD execution?
options: Two cores running unrelated programs
One AVX instruction adding eight pairs of numbers at once
Redundant computers checking each other's results on the same input
A cluster of nodes exchanging MPI messages
questions.explanation: SIMD applies one instruction to multiple data elements. CPU vector extensions such as SSE, AVX and NEON, and vector processors, are classic SIMD hardware.

questions.text: A Symmetric Multi-Processing (SMP) system has two or more _ processors connected to a single ___ main memory.
options: identical; shared
dissimilar; shared
dissimilar; distributed
identical; distributed
questions.explanation: In SMP all processors are equal peers with the same view of one shared memory, and any of them can run any thread.

questions.text: A CPU has 8 physical cores, each with 2-way simultaneous multithreading (SMT). How many logical CPUs does the OS see?
questions.explanation: Each SMT context appears to the OS as a logical CPU. The 16 contexts still share only 8 cores' execution units and caches.

questions.text: Compared with a processor that has 8 physical cores, a hyperthreaded processor with 8 logical cores (4 physical) usually provides _____ performance.
options: lower
higher
identical
double
questions.explanation: SMT threads share one core's execution units, caches and bandwidth. SMT improves utilisation when one thread stalls, but it does not match a second physical core.

questions.text: In modern multicore CPUs, what normally keeps the cores' cached copies of memory consistent?
options: The application, by flushing its caches manually after writes
The operating system, during every context switch
The processor hardware, through a cache-coherence protocol
The compiler, by inserting copy instructions
questions.explanation: Coherence is maintained transparently by hardware, typically with a MESI-style protocol. Software sees one consistent value per cache line without managing copies itself.

questions.text: What does a cache-coherence protocol such as MESI coordinate?
options: The order in which threads are scheduled on cores
The states of each line's cached copies across cores
Which program may allocate physical memory next
The clock frequency and voltage of each core
questions.explanation: Cores must agree on each line's value, so lines are tracked as Modified, Exclusive, Shared or Invalid. A write invalidates other cores' copies, which keeps them consistent but generates coherence traffic.

questions.text: Which of these applications would benefit most from parallel execution on multiple cores?
options: A tool that downloads several files from the Internet
A math library that processes large matrices
A logging service that frequently writes to a database
A GUI form for an accounting application
questions.explanation: Large matrix operations are CPU-bound and split naturally into independent pieces. The downloader and logger are mostly I/O-bound, so concurrency helps them more than parallel computation.

questions.text: What is a cache line?
options: The bus that connects the L1 cache to main memory
The fixed-size block, often 64 bytes, that caches transfer
A queue of pending requests waiting for the cache
A register that counts cache hits and misses
questions.explanation: Caches load and track whole lines, not individual bytes. This is why nearby data is cheap to access and why unrelated variables can share a line.

questions.text: What is false sharing?
options: Two threads reading invalid data because of a race
Threads writing separate variables on the same cache line
One thread reading memory that belongs to another process
A security flaw that leaks cache contents across cores
questions.explanation: The variables are logically independent, but the cache line keeps moving between cores. False sharing can slow a program even when it has no data race.

questions.text: Each worker thread increments its own counter, but the counters sit next to each other in one array and the program scales poorly. What is a likely fix?
options: Protect all the counters with one mutex
Give each worker's counter its own cache line
Declare every counter as volatile
Add more worker threads to spread the load
questions.explanation: Adjacent counters share cache lines, so every increment invalidates other cores' copies. Padding them apart, or keeping local counts and combining them at the end, removes that traffic.

questions.text: Does hardware cache coherence make unsynchronized concurrent code correct?
options: Yes, coherence guarantees every thread sees writes in program order
No, ordering still needs atomics, locks or other synchronization
Yes, but only on x86 processors with strong ordering
No, because coherence is disabled when several threads run
questions.explanation: Coherence keeps each cache line consistent, but compilers and CPUs still reorder operations. The language memory model, through synchronization, is what defines correct ordering.

questions.text: How do UMA and NUMA architectures differ?
options: UMA is found only in single-core processors
UMA access time is uniform; in NUMA it depends on location
NUMA systems cannot offer a shared address space
NUMA uses faster memory chips than UMA systems
questions.explanation: In NUMA, memory is attached to particular sockets or nodes, and local accesses are faster than remote ones. Modern multi-socket servers are typically cache-coherent NUMA.

questions.text: On a Linux NUMA server, one thread initialises a large array and then 32 threads on two sockets process it. Why might the threads on one socket run slower?
options: The other socket's cores have a lower clock speed
First-touch placed every page on the initialising thread's node
NUMA prevents two sockets from reading the same array
Only one socket at a time can use its L1 caches
questions.explanation: By default a page lives on the node of the thread that first touches it, so the other socket's accesses are remote. Initialising data in parallel, with the same threads that will use it, keeps accesses local.

questions.text: What is the purpose of a memory barrier (fence)?
options: To protect memory from unauthorised access
To allocate a new block of aligned memory
To limit how memory operations may be reordered
To flush the entire CPU cache to disk
questions.explanation: A fence stops the compiler and CPU from reordering certain loads and stores across it. Atomics with acquire or release ordering provide the same kind of guarantee in a structured way.

questions.text: What is branch prediction?
options: The compiler choosing which branch of an if to compile
The CPU guessing a branch's outcome to keep fetching instructions
Predicting which memory addresses a program will access next
Running both sides of every branch on different cores
questions.explanation: A correct guess keeps the pipeline full. A misprediction forces the CPU to discard the speculative work and refill the pipeline, costing many cycles.

questions.text: What is speculative execution?
options: Running only the code the programmer marked as optional
Executing instructions before knowing they are needed, undoing wrong guesses
A debugging mode that executes every instruction twice to check it
A compiler optimisation that deletes code it predicts will be unused
questions.explanation: Combined with branch prediction, speculation lets the CPU work ahead. Only correctly predicted results are committed to the architectural state.

questions.text: What does out-of-order execution do?
options: Executes the program's statements in a random order each run
Runs independent instructions as soon as their inputs are ready
Reorders the source code once at compile time
Executes instructions backwards to undo earlier mistakes
questions.explanation: While one instruction waits, for example on a cache miss, later independent instructions can run. Retiring in order preserves the program's visible behavior on that core.

questions.text: What is instruction-level parallelism (ILP)?
options: Running several programs at once on several cores
One core executing several independent instructions at once
Splitting one instruction across several cores
Parallelism between different programming languages
questions.explanation: Pipelining, superscalar issue and out-of-order execution exploit ILP. Data dependencies between instructions limit how much is available.

questions.text: How do the L1, L2 and L3 caches typically compare?
options: They are the same size but store different kinds of data
L1 is smallest and fastest; L3 is largest and slowest
L3 is fastest because it is closest to memory
L1 is shared by all cores, while L3 is private to each core
questions.explanation: Each level trades speed for capacity, with L2 in between. L1 is usually private to a core, while L3 is often shared by several or all cores.

questions.text: What is a GPU's architecture optimised for?
options: Running operating-system code with low latency
Fast execution of single-threaded, branch-heavy programs
High throughput on many similar, independent operations
Managing file systems and storage devices
questions.explanation: A GPU keeps many lightweight threads in flight and switches between them to hide memory latency. CPUs invest more hardware in making a few threads fast.

questions.text: When can offloading a computation to a GPU make it slower than running it on the CPU?
options: Whenever the data is stored in floating point
When the problem is small and data transfers dominate
Whenever the CPU has more than eight cores
When the algorithm is perfectly data-parallel
questions.explanation: A GPU is not automatically faster. Transfer cost, small problem size, branch divergence and low arithmetic intensity can all remove the benefit.

questions.text: What does GPGPU computing mean?
options: Using a GPU only for rendering games and video
Using GPUs for general-purpose, non-graphics computation
A shading language for writing graphics effects
A tool for debugging graphics drivers on Linux
questions.explanation: Programming models such as CUDA, HIP, OpenCL and SYCL let GPUs run simulations, linear algebra and machine learning workloads.

questions.text: What best describes the difference between latency and throughput?
options: Latency is work per second; throughput is the time for one operation
Latency is time per operation; throughput is work per unit time
Latency matters only for GPUs; throughput only for CPUs
Both measure the same thing in different units
questions.explanation: A system can process many items per second while each item still takes a long time. CPUs lean towards low latency, GPUs towards high throughput.

questions.text: How are data parallelism and SIMD related?
options: They are two names for the same hardware feature
Data parallelism is a workload property; SIMD is one way to exploit it
SIMD is a workload property; data parallelism is a CPU instruction set
Data parallelism requires a GPU, while SIMD requires a cluster
questions.explanation: Applying the same operation to many elements can be executed with SIMD instructions, GPU threads in SIMT groups or multiple cores.

questions.text: What is a vector processor?
options: A processor dedicated to drawing vector graphics on screen
A processor whose instructions operate on whole vectors of elements
A processor with many independent, identical cores
A processor that only performs integer arithmetic
questions.explanation: One vector instruction streams many elements through deep pipelines, so a new element can enter every cycle after start-up. Long vectors use the hardware best.

questions.text: What is cache thrashing?
options: Deliberately clearing the cache to improve security
Repeated misses as data is evicted before it can be reused
Two caches exchanging lines faster than memory can
A cache optimisation that prefetches data in bulk
questions.explanation: Thrashing happens when the working set does not fit, or when access patterns map many addresses to the same cache sets. Performance then approaches that of main memory.

questions.text: How do shared-memory and distributed-memory systems differ?
options: Shared memory is always faster; distributed memory is always slower
Shared: one address space; distributed: per-node memory and messages
Shared memory is used for small data; distributed memory for large data
There is no practical difference for programmers
questions.explanation: Shared memory lets threads communicate through loads and stores. Distributed memory scales further but requires explicit message passing, for example with MPI.

questions.text: What is memory bandwidth?
options: The total amount of installed memory
The rate at which data can be read from or written to memory
The delay before the first byte of a request arrives
The number of memory addresses a program may use
questions.explanation: Bandwidth is measured in bytes per second and limits data-heavy workloads. The delay for one access is latency, a separate property.

questions.text: A memory-bound loop already saturates DRAM bandwidth with 8 cores. What usually happens if you run it on 16 cores?
options: It becomes about twice as fast, like compute-bound code
It barely speeds up, since bandwidth is already saturated
It always slows down to exactly half its speed
It becomes compute-bound and scales linearly
questions.explanation: All cores share finite memory bandwidth. Once it is saturated, extra cores add compute capacity that the loop cannot use.

questions.text: What is hardware prefetching?
options: Loading a program into memory before it is started
Loading data into cache before the program requests it
Compiling frequently used functions ahead of time
Reordering data in memory so it is sorted
questions.explanation: Prefetchers recognise patterns such as sequential or strided access. Predictable access patterns therefore run much faster than random ones.

questions.text: What is the "memory wall"?
options: A physical limit on how much RAM a single machine can hold
The growing gap between processor speed and memory access speed
A hardware barrier that isolates each process's memory from others
A cache that blocks writes from reaching memory
questions.explanation: Processors improved faster than DRAM latency for decades, so many programs spend much of their time waiting for memory. Caches, prefetching and locality-aware code help.

questions.text: With a write-back cache policy, when is modified data written to main memory?
options: Immediately, as part of every store
When the dirty line is evicted or flushed
Only when the owning program exits
Never, because the cache replaces main memory
questions.explanation: Write-back avoids writing to memory on every store, saving bandwidth. A write-through cache, by contrast, updates memory on every write.

questions.text: Which of these describes a program's latency?
options: The ratio of sequential to parallel execution time
The time one task takes to complete
The number of tasks completed per unit of time
The number of processors the program uses
questions.explanation: Latency is measured per operation, from start to finish. Percentiles such as p95 and p99 are often reported because an average can hide slow outliers.

questions.text: Which of these describes a program's throughput?
options: The number of tasks completed per unit of time
The ratio of sequential to parallel execution time
The time one task takes to complete
The number of processors the program uses
questions.explanation: Throughput counts completed work per second, such as requests or images. A system can raise throughput without lowering the latency of any single task.

questions.text: Which of these describes a program's speedup?
options: The time one task takes to complete
One-processor time divided by p-processor time
The number of tasks completed per unit of time
The number of processors the program uses
questions.explanation: Speedup is S_p = T_1 / T_p, based on wall-clock time for the same problem. A speedup of p is linear, or ideal, speedup.

questions.text: 85% of a program's runtime is parallelizable and runs 6 times faster on a 6-core processor. According to Amdahl's Law, what is the overall speedup?
options: About 3.43
About 4.62
About 5.10
Exactly 6.00
questions.explanation: S = 1 / ((1 - 0.85) + 0.85/6) = 1 / (0.15 + 0.142) ≈ 3.43. The 15% serial portion keeps the result well below the core count.

questions.text: Amdahl's Law gives a(n) _____ on the overall speedup from parallelizing a program.
options: lower limit
upper limit
average value
exact prediction
questions.explanation: The model assumes the parallel part divides perfectly and ignores communication, synchronization and imbalance. Real programs therefore do no better than it predicts, and usually worse.

questions.text: If 95% of a fixed-size program can be parallelized, what is the maximum speedup with unlimited processors, according to Amdahl's Law?
questions.explanation: As the processor count grows, the speedup approaches 1 / (1 - P) = 1 / 0.05 = 20. The 5% serial part takes the same time no matter how many processors are added.

questions.text: How does Gustafson's Law differ from Amdahl's Law?
options: It applies only to shared-memory machines
It lets the problem grow with the processor count
It assumes the serial fraction grows with p
It gives a lower bound instead of an upper bound
questions.explanation: Amdahl asks how much faster a fixed problem can run. Gustafson asks how much larger a problem can be solved in about the same time, giving a more optimistic, weak-scaling view.

questions.text: A scaled workload has a serial fraction of 0.05. What speedup does Gustafson's Law predict on 32 processors?
options: About 12.5
About 20.0
About 30.45
Exactly 32.0
questions.explanation: Gustafson's scaled speedup is p - α(p - 1) = 32 - 0.05 × 31 = 30.45. Because the parallel work grows with p, the serial part matters much less than under Amdahl's Law.

questions.text: A computation takes 100 seconds on one processor and 28 seconds on four. What is its parallel efficiency?
options: About 28%
About 72%
About 89%
About 357%
questions.explanation: Speedup is 100 / 28 ≈ 3.57, and efficiency is speedup divided by processor count: 3.57 / 4 ≈ 0.89. An efficiency near 100% means near-linear speedup.

questions.text: As more processors are applied to a fixed-size problem, what typically happens to parallel efficiency?
options: It stays constant at 100%
It rises steadily along with speedup
It falls, even while speedup may still increase
It becomes exactly zero beyond 8 processors
questions.explanation: Serial work, communication and synchronization stay roughly constant or grow while each processor's share of useful work shrinks, so each added processor contributes less.

questions.text: What is superlinear speedup, and what can cause it?
options: Speedup below 1, caused by too much communication
Speedup above p, often because each part now fits in cache
Speedup exactly equal to p, from perfect load balance
An impossible result that always indicates a timing bug
questions.explanation: Splitting the problem shrinks each worker's working set, which can cut cache misses or paging. The parallel run then does less memory work per element than the one-processor baseline.

questions.text: What is an advantage of fine-grained parallelism with many small tasks?
options: A high computation-to-communication ratio
Lower scheduling overhead
Good load balancing
Better cache locality
questions.explanation: Many small tasks can be spread evenly and rebalanced dynamically. The cost is more frequent scheduling, synchronization and communication.

questions.text: What is an advantage of coarse-grained parallelism with a few large tasks?
options: A high computation-to-communication ratio
Good load balancing for irregular work
More tasks available than processors
Easier recovery from slow tasks
questions.explanation: Large tasks do more computation between coordination events, so overhead is a smaller fraction of runtime. If a few tasks run long, though, other processors sit idle.

questions.text: Granularity can be described as the ratio of _ to ___.
options: speedup; number of processors
tasks; time
tasks; number of processors
computation; communication
questions.explanation: Granularity compares useful work in a task with its coordination cost. A task must do enough work to amortise the cost of scheduling and communicating it.

questions.text: In a computational graph, which of these describes the critical path?
options: The longest chain of dependent operations through the program
The total time of all task nodes in the graph
The shortest path from the start node to the end node
The set of tasks that access shared memory
questions.explanation: Operations on the critical path must run one after another, so its length bounds the execution time no matter how many processors are available.

questions.text: In a computational graph, which of these describes a program's work?
options: The time of the task nodes along the critical path
The longest chain of dependent operations
The total time of all task nodes in the graph
The number of edges between task nodes
questions.explanation: Work, T_1, is the time a single processor needs to execute every task. It is the total amount of computation, regardless of how it is scheduled.

questions.text: In a computational graph, which of these describes a program's span?
options: The total time of all task nodes in the graph
The total time of the task nodes along the critical path
The number of processors needed to run the graph
The time between the first and second task nodes
questions.explanation: Span, T_∞, is the execution time with unlimited processors. It equals the length of the critical path.

questions.text: What does the ratio of work to span represent?
options: The communication overhead paid per processor
The parallelism, an upper bound on achievable speedup
The fraction of the program that must run serially
The number of tasks that are on the critical path
questions.explanation: Because span is part of the work, the ratio is always at least 1. A ratio of 1 means no parallelism; larger values mean more processors can be used profitably.

questions.text: Why are computational graphs useful when designing a parallel program?
options: They automatically eliminate data races between tasks
They show which tasks depend on which, exposing parallelism
They replace the need to measure performance later
They pinpoint exactly which lines of code need a mutex
questions.explanation: Tasks with no path between them in the graph are independent and can run concurrently. The graph also exposes the critical path that limits speedup.

questions.text: Increasing the number of processors while keeping the problem size per processor fixed (weak scaling) aims to accomplish _ in ___.
options: the same work; less time
more work; the same time
more work; less time
less work; the same time
questions.explanation: In weak scaling the total problem grows with the machine. Ideally the runtime stays constant while the total amount of work increases.

questions.text: Increasing the number of processors while keeping the total problem size fixed (strong scaling) aims to accomplish _ in ___.
options: more work; less time
the same work; less time
more work; the same time
less work; more time
questions.explanation: Strong scaling divides a fixed problem among more processors. It eventually saturates when each processor's share becomes too small relative to overhead.

questions.text: Why should you repeat a timing measurement several times and report the variation?
options: The system clock drifts randomly between runs
The first run always crashes on parallel machines
Scheduling, caches and background load vary between runs
Averaging makes the program itself run faster
questions.explanation: Scheduling, cache state, frequency scaling and background activity all change runtimes. Repeated runs, with warm-up handled consistently, show typical behavior and how much it varies.

questions.text: A parallel run on 4 processors takes 30 seconds, and the one-processor baseline takes 100 seconds. What is the total parallel overhead, T_o = p·T_p − T_1?
options: 0 seconds
20 seconds
70 seconds
120 seconds
questions.explanation: The parallel run consumes 4 × 30 = 120 processor-seconds, while the useful work is 100 seconds. The extra 20 seconds are communication, synchronization, idle time and other overhead.

questions.text: What does the scalability of a parallel program describe?
options: How large its source code can grow over time
How its performance changes as resources are added
The maximum number of threads its language allows
How many users can download and install it at once
questions.explanation: A scalable program keeps gaining useful performance as resources grow. Scalability is measured experimentally, for example with strong- and weak-scaling studies.

questions.text: What is load imbalance?
options: A power supply that cannot sustain the processors' load
Uneven work, so some processors wait while others are busy
Too much total work for the machine's memory to hold
A network link carrying more traffic than another
questions.explanation: In synchronized programs the slowest worker sets the runtime. Dynamic scheduling, work stealing or finer-grained tasks can improve balance.

questions.text: Four workers finish a phase in 10, 10, 10 and 30 seconds. What is the imbalance ratio, T_max / T_avg?
questions.explanation: The average is 60 / 4 = 15 seconds, and 30 / 15 = 2.0. A ratio of 1.0 would mean perfect balance; here three workers sit idle for 20 seconds each.

questions.text: What does isoefficiency describe?
options: Every processor in a system having equal efficiency
How fast problem size must grow with p to keep efficiency fixed
The energy used per operation by a parallel computer
The efficiency of a program's reads and writes to disk
questions.explanation: A slowly growing isoefficiency function means the algorithm scales well: modest increases in problem size keep added processors productive.

questions.text: A program uses 4 threads and finishes in 10 seconds of elapsed time, consuming about 40 seconds of CPU time. Which time should be used to compute its speedup?
options: The 10 seconds of wall-clock time
The 40 seconds of CPU time
The CPU time divided by the number of threads
The CPU time of the slowest thread only
questions.explanation: Speedup is about how long the user waits, which is elapsed wall-clock time. CPU time adds up across threads and can increase even as the program gets faster.

questions.text: Why do larger problems often achieve better parallel speedup than small ones?
options: Larger problems always contain less serial code
Fixed overheads become a smaller share of the total work
Larger problems run at a higher clock frequency
Small problems cannot be split across processors at all
questions.explanation: Communication and start-up costs matter relatively less as useful work per processor grows. This is the effect Gustafson's Law and weak scaling describe.

questions.text: What is the main purpose of profiling a parallel program?
options: To create performance profiles for different users
To find where time goes, including waiting, before optimising
To test the program for security vulnerabilities
To list every hardware platform the program supports
questions.explanation: In parallel programs, time is often lost in locks, barriers, communication or imbalance rather than in the hottest function. Measure first, then optimise the measured bottleneck.

questions.text: How does sampling profiling differ from instrumentation?
options: Sampling records the location periodically; instrumentation adds measurement code
Sampling requires recompiling the whole program; instrumentation never does
Sampling can measure only GPU code; instrumentation only CPU code
They are two names for the same profiling technique
questions.explanation: Tools such as perf sample, which barely disturbs timing. Instrumentation, as with gprof or Callgrind, records every call but can change the behavior it measures.

questions.text: What does the roofline model show?
options: The physical height limit of racks in a data centre
Performance bounds set by peak compute and memory bandwidth
The network topology connecting the nodes of a cluster
The cost of a machine relative to its performance
questions.explanation: It plots attainable performance against arithmetic intensity. Kernels with low intensity sit under the sloped memory-bandwidth roof; those with high intensity hit the flat compute roof. It shows which limit to attack.

questions.text: What is arithmetic intensity?
options: How complicated a program's mathematical formulas are
Operations performed per byte moved from memory
The clock speed of the arithmetic units
The number of arithmetic units in a processor
questions.explanation: High arithmetic intensity means each byte loaded is reused for much computation, so the code is more likely to be compute-bound than memory-bound.

questions.text: When timing an MPI phase, why is the maximum elapsed time across ranks reported, for example with MPI_Reduce and MPI_MAX?
options: The maximum is always the most accurate single measurement
The phase is not complete until the slowest rank finishes
Rank 0 cannot measure its own time
MPI timers only work on the slowest rank
questions.explanation: Averaging per-rank times would hide stragglers. The parallel phase ends when every rank has finished, so the slowest one determines its duration.

questions.text: A program reports 100% CPU utilisation on every core but shows poor speedup. How is this possible?
options: It is not possible, since full utilisation guarantees linear speedup
The cores may be busy spinning on locks, missing in cache or doing redundant work
Utilisation counters are always inaccurate on multicore CPUs
Speedup cannot be measured when utilisation is 100%
questions.explanation: Busy is not the same as productive. Interpret utilisation together with throughput, efficiency and hardware counters to see whether the cycles are doing useful work.

questions.text: Why can timing only the host call that launches a GPU kernel be misleading?
options: Kernel launches always take exactly the same time as the kernel
The launch returns before the kernel finishes running
GPU kernels cannot be timed from the host at all
The host clock is paused while a kernel runs
questions.explanation: The timer captures only submission. Use GPU events for device time, or synchronize before stopping a host timer. Also state whether data transfers and allocation are included.

questions.text: In a strong-scaling study, what is the "scaling knee"?
options: The processor count at which the program first produces correct output
The point beyond which adding processors gives little further improvement
The processor count at which power consumption is highest
The point where efficiency first exceeds 100%
questions.explanation: Plotting runtime, speedup and efficiency against processor count shows where gains flatten out. Running past the knee wastes resources for that workload and configuration.

questions.text: What are the four stages of Foster's PCAM parallel design methodology?
options: Planning, Coding, Analysis, Monitoring
Partitioning, Communication, Agglomeration, Mapping
Preparation, Computation, Aggregation, Merging
Partitioning, Combination, Assignment, Measurement
questions.explanation: Partitioning splits the work into tasks, communication identifies the data they exchange, agglomeration groups tasks, and mapping assigns them to processors.

questions.text: Which stage of the parallel design process focuses on breaking the problem down into discrete pieces of work?
options: Mapping
Agglomeration
Communication
Partitioning
questions.explanation: Partitioning exposes the available parallelism, ideally producing many more potential tasks than processors so later stages have flexibility.

questions.text: Which stage of the parallel design process focuses on what data tasks must exchange and how they coordinate?
options: Mapping
Agglomeration
Partitioning
Communication
questions.explanation: The communication stage identifies which tasks need each other's results and how they exchange them, distinguishing data movement from synchronization.

questions.text: Which stage of the parallel design process combines small tasks into larger ones, possibly replicating data or computation, to improve efficiency?
options: Mapping
Agglomeration
Communication
Partitioning
questions.explanation: Agglomeration increases granularity, reducing communication and scheduling overhead, while keeping enough tasks to balance the load.

questions.text: Which stage of the parallel design process specifies where each task will execute?
options: Communication
Mapping
Agglomeration
Partitioning
questions.explanation: Mapping assigns tasks to cores, sockets, nodes or accelerators to balance load and keep frequently communicating tasks close together.

questions.text: Why does the partitioning stage come before the communication stage?
options: Tasks must be grouped into larger units first
The division of work determines what data must be exchanged
Each task's physical location must be known first
The order of the four stages is arbitrary
questions.explanation: Communication needs depend on the dependencies between the tasks produced by partitioning. Grouping happens later, in agglomeration, and placement in mapping.

questions.text: How should the PCAM stages be applied in practice?
options: Strictly once and in order, never revisiting an earlier stage
Iteratively, revisiting earlier stages when later ones expose problems
In any order, since the stages do not affect each other
Only the mapping stage is still needed on modern hardware
questions.explanation: For example, a mapping may reveal that communication is too costly, prompting different agglomeration or partitioning. The final design should be validated by measurement.

questions.text: Why do programmers often skip explicit mapping for threads on a typical desktop operating system?
options: The OS scheduler assigns threads to cores automatically
Desktop computers have too few cores for mapping to matter
Desktop operating systems forbid choosing a thread's core
Mapping only applies to GPU programs
questions.explanation: The scheduler places and migrates threads dynamically. Affinity and pinning can still matter for performance, especially on NUMA or HPC systems.

questions.text: What is domain decomposition?
options: Splitting a program into modules by business domain
Dividing the data into chunks that workers process alike
Dividing a problem by the different operations it performs
Separating the problem domain from the solution domain
questions.explanation: Each worker owns a region of the data. It works well when computation is mostly local, as in image filters, simulations and matrix operations.

questions.text: A 2D grid is split among four workers. Why do 2×2 square tiles usually communicate less than four thin strips?
options: Square tiles contain fewer grid points in total
Tiles have less boundary per area, so less halo exchange
Thin strips cannot be processed in parallel at all
Square tiles never need any ghost cells
questions.explanation: Computation grows with a tile's area, while communication grows with its perimeter. For an N×N grid, the cuts total 2N for tiles but 3N for strips.

questions.text: What is functional decomposition?
options: Splitting functions into smaller helper functions
Dividing a problem by the different operations it performs
Dividing a dataset into equal contiguous blocks
Removing unused functions to shrink the program
questions.explanation: For example, a web request can pass through authentication, database, formatting and rendering stages, each handled by its own workers. This naturally forms pipelines.

questions.text: A three-stage pipeline takes 2 ms, 5 ms and 3 ms per item, with one worker per stage. What is its steady-state throughput?
options: 100 items per second
200 items per second
333 items per second
500 items per second
questions.explanation: Once the pipeline is full, the slowest stage completes one item every 5 ms, so throughput is 200 items per second. Each item's latency is still 10 ms.

questions.text: What is the difference between data parallelism and task parallelism?
options: Data parallelism is always faster than task parallelism on CPUs
Data: same operation on different data; task: different operations at once
Task parallelism always uses more memory than data parallelism
Data parallelism applies only to database queries
questions.explanation: An image filter applied to every pixel is data-parallel; serving unrelated requests or running pipeline stages at once is task-parallel. Real programs often combine both.

questions.text: What is an embarrassingly parallel computation?
options: A computation too simple to be worth parallelizing
One made of independent tasks needing little or no communication
A poorly designed algorithm that parallelizes badly in practice
A computation that always contains hidden race conditions
questions.explanation: Rendering separate frames or running independent Monte Carlo trials are examples. Such workloads usually scale well, limited mainly by load balance and I/O.

questions.text: What does a divide-and-conquer algorithm do when it reaches the base case?
options: Stops subdividing and solves the subproblem directly
Recursively solves a set of smaller subproblems
Merges all of the subproblems created so far
Divides the problem into two smaller subproblems
questions.explanation: The base case ends the recursion. In parallel versions, a cutoff on problem size also stops creating tasks too small to be worth scheduling.

questions.text: What is the master-worker (manager-worker) pattern?
options: Every process does identical work with no coordination
One process hands out tasks to workers and collects results
Workers elect a new master every time a task finishes
A pattern used only for handling errors in workers
questions.explanation: The master hands out tasks and gathers results, which balances load naturally. With many workers, the master itself can become a bottleneck.

questions.text: What is the bag-of-tasks (work queue) pattern?
options: Giving every worker a fixed list of tasks up front
Workers repeatedly take the next task from a shared pool
Storing completed results in an unordered collection
Running every task on every worker for redundancy
questions.explanation: Load balances dynamically: fast workers simply take more tasks, so uneven task costs balance out. Contention on the shared queue can limit scaling with many workers.

questions.text: What is work stealing?
options: A security attack in which a process takes another's CPU time
Idle workers take tasks from the queues of busy workers
A scheduler that cancels slow tasks and restarts them elsewhere
A type of race condition in task queues
questions.explanation: Each worker mostly uses its own deque, so there is no central bottleneck. Only idle workers steal, which keeps contention low while balancing load.

questions.text: How does static load balancing differ from dynamic load balancing?
options: Static is meant for unchanging data; dynamic is for data that changes
Static assigns work before execution; dynamic redistributes work during execution
Static is always faster, while dynamic is always more accurate
Static uses threads; dynamic uses processes
questions.explanation: Static mapping has no run-time overhead and suits uniform, predictable work. Dynamic mapping handles irregular task costs but adds scheduling overhead and may reduce locality.

questions.text: What is the fork-join model?
options: A model for committing database transactions
A task splits into parallel subtasks, then waits for all of them
A pattern in which child processes duplicate the parent's open files
A network protocol for joining new nodes to a running cluster
questions.explanation: Parallel regions open and close around independent work, as in OpenMP parallel loops or recursive parallel merge sort.

questions.text: What is the SPMD (Single Program, Multiple Data) model?
options: Each processor runs a different program on the same data
Every processor runs the same program on different data
One processor runs the program while others store data
A hardware design in which one instruction controls all cores
questions.explanation: Most MPI programs are SPMD: every rank runs the same executable and uses its rank to select its portion of the data or role.

questions.text: What is speculative parallelism?
options: Running parallel algorithms that have not been tested
Doing work in parallel before knowing whether it is needed
Assigning tasks to processors at random to save time
Estimating a program's speedup without running it
questions.explanation: For example, both branches of a costly decision can be computed while the condition is evaluated. Unneeded results are discarded, trading extra work for lower latency.

questions.text: What characterises the bulk synchronous parallel (BSP) model?
options: Processes communicate continuously without synchronizing
Supersteps of local computation, communication and a barrier
All data is processed in one large batch on a single processor
A hardware architecture built around one shared bus
questions.explanation: Within a superstep, processes compute on local data and send messages. The barrier at the end makes the messages available for the next superstep.

questions.text: Which loop cannot be parallelized by simply splitting its iterations among threads?
options: for i in range(n): c[i] = a[i] + b[i]
for i in range(1, n): a[i] = a[i - 1] + b[i]
for i in range(n): b[i] = 2 * a[i]
for i in range(n): c[i] = max(a[i], b[i])
questions.explanation: Each iteration needs the result of the previous one, a loop-carried dependency. The others are independent per index; this one needs a restructured algorithm such as a parallel scan.

questions.text: What is a stencil computation?
options: A code template that new parallel programs are written from
Updating each grid element from a fixed pattern of its neighbors
A tool for drawing a program's task dependency graph
A protocol for broadcasting data from one root
questions.explanation: Heat diffusion and image blurs are stencils. In parallel versions, each worker needs halo data from neighbors at its boundaries every step.

questions.text: What is a reduction in parallel computing?
options: Reducing the number of processors to save power
Combining many values into one, using an operation like sum
Simplifying parallel code by removing all its locks
Reducing a program's peak memory usage by compression
questions.explanation: The operation, such as sum or max, must be associative. Workers compute partial results locally, then combine them, typically in a tree, which takes logarithmic steps instead of a serial loop.

questions.text: What does a prefix sum (scan) compute for the input [3, 1, 4, 2]?
questions.explanation: An inclusive scan gives the running total at every position. It can be computed in parallel and is a building block for many parallel algorithms.

questions.text: Why does data locality matter in parallel design?
options: It keeps data stored in local files rather than databases
Using nearby data cuts communication and memory traffic
It guarantees that no synchronization is needed
It is a security measure that hides data from other processes
questions.explanation: Accessing nearby data is far cheaper than fetching it from another core's cache, another NUMA node or another machine. Good partitioning and mapping keep most accesses local.

questions.text: What does the "owner computes" rule state?
options: The processor that compiled the code must execute it
The owner of each piece of data computes its updates
Only the master process may write the final results
Every processor computes every value and compares results
questions.explanation: Assigning computation by data ownership keeps writes local and makes clear which process must send or receive boundary values.

questions.text: In a task dependency graph, what do the edges represent?
options: The physical links between processors
Data or ordering dependencies between tasks
The memory each task allocates
The order in which the programmer wrote the tasks
questions.explanation: Tasks without a path between them can run concurrently. The longest path, the critical path, limits the minimum execution time.

questions.text: What is block decomposition of an array?
options: Splitting source code into separate compilation blocks
Giving each worker one or more contiguous chunks of the array
Assigning individual elements to workers in round-robin order
Blocking all workers until the array is ready
questions.explanation: Contiguous blocks give good cache locality and simple index arithmetic. They balance poorly when some regions are much more expensive to process than others.

questions.text: With cyclic decomposition, item i goes to worker i mod P. With 4 workers, which worker processes item 10?
options: Worker 0
Worker 1
Worker 2
Worker 3
questions.explanation: 10 mod 4 = 2. Round-robin assignment spreads expensive items across workers, improving balance at the cost of locality.

questions.text: Why is block-cyclic decomposition often used in distributed dense linear algebra?
options: It eliminates all communication between processes
It balances load while keeping locality within blocks
It assigns the whole matrix to the fastest process
It needs no knowledge of the matrix dimensions
questions.explanation: Blocks are dealt round-robin. Pure block layouts can leave some processes idle as the active region shrinks, and pure cyclic layouts lose locality. Block-cyclic is a compromise between the two.

questions.text: Message time is often modelled as α + n/B (startup latency plus size over bandwidth). What does this suggest about sending 1,000 tiny messages?
options: It costs the same as one message with the same total bytes
Latency is paid 1,000 times, so batching them is usually faster
Small messages are always faster because they use less bandwidth
Only the bandwidth term matters for small messages
questions.explanation: For small messages the fixed latency term dominates. Batching data reduces the number of startups paid, which is why agglomeration reduces communication cost.

questions.text: What is the goal of graph partitioning when mapping irregular tasks?
options: To give every partition the same number of edges
To balance work while cutting few communication edges
To place each task on its own separate processor
To remove all dependencies from the task graph
questions.explanation: Each cut edge represents communication between processors. Partitioners for meshes and sparse matrices balance the work per part while keeping cuts small.

questions.text: A stencil code uses nonblocking communication to overlap halo exchange with work. Which order of steps achieves this?
options: Wait for the halos, then post receives, then compute every point
Post receives and sends, compute the interior, wait for halos, then compute the boundary
Compute the boundary, then the interior, and finally post receives
Post receives, wait on them at once, then send the boundary data out
questions.explanation: Interior points do not depend on halo data, so they can be computed while messages are in flight. Only the boundary update must wait for the received values.
